title: When And Why It's Okay For Students To Talk
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin pushes back on the idea that good classroom management requires constant silence, arguing that rigid quiet only breeds boredom, resentment, and a dislike of school. He distinguishes between necessary quiet periods, such as independent work, and the rest of the day, when students need built-in breaks to recharge. While physical movement breaks like jumping jacks or dancing can help, he identifies structured talking breaks as the most effective reset. The key, he explains, is that the teacher — not the students — defines and models what the break looks like, including clear start and stop signals and a set time limit of two to four minutes. Done this way, talking breaks leave students calmer, more focused, and more receptive when instruction resumes. The article frames brief, teacher-directed talk time as a simple tool that channels restlessness productively rather than undermining classroom order.
points: Constant, rigid silence is not the same as good classroom management — it causes boredom, resentment, and dislike of school.
Uninterrupted independent work time is a legitimate reason for quiet, but it is an academic strategy, not a control tactic.
Structured, teacher-modeled talking breaks of two to four minutes are one of the most effective ways to reset student energy.
The talking break must be defined and demonstrated by the teacher first — letting ongoing chatter continue only makes things worse.
Bookending the break with clear start and stop signals helps students return to work more receptive, energized, and focused.
quotes: There is a common misconception that effective classroom management means silence.
It causes boredom, resentment, and a strong dislike for school. It makes every day an agonizing, tension-filled slog to dismissal.
To create a healthy, well-behaved environment, your students need breaks. They need opportunities to stretch their legs and recharge their batteries.
Now, it’s important to point out that letting students continue to talk because that’s what they’re already doing is a bad idea and will only make matters worse.
You lay out your expectations by showing precisely what is and isn’t okay. A reminder that you’ll follow your classroom management plan as usual is also a good idea.
Giving students a few minutes to talk with their friends is a simple little thing. But it effectively shakes the restlessness out of their system.
It settles. It calms. It motivates. It prepares them for the challenges that lie ahead.
